usage: wl [-h] [--version] [--db PATH] [--color {auto,always,never}]
          [--theme {auto,dark,light,mono}] [--width {full,help,N}] [--title {wrap,clip}] [-q]
          [--no-brief] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [--log-format {oneline,full}] [--show-canceled]
          <command> ...

worklog (wl) — a fast, local, SQLite-backed worklog & planner.
Track tasks/projects, log progress, plan your day, and review — all from the shell.

New here? Try:  wl init  →  wl add "my first task"  →  wl log 1 "made progress"  →  wl day
Run wl <command> -h for any command's options + examples. Commands are grouped by purpose at the
bottom of this help.

positional arguments:
  <command>
    migrate             apply pending SQL migrations from migrations/NNNN_*.sql (auto-run on every
                        command; this is the explicit form)
    doctor              check the node graph for inconsistencies no foreign key prevents (dangling
                        parent, cycles, orphan spokes, dead/one-sided/self relations, date-only log
                        timestamps)
    config              print resolved configuration: DB path, aliases path, XDG dirs, env vars,
                        embedding
    init                initialize SQLite DB (default ~/.local/share/worklog/worklog.db; skips if it
                        exists)
    demo                seed a sample 'a day with wl' dataset — EMPTY database only
    add                 create a new node (task/project/area/meetlog/habit/day...); compound flags
                        let you do add + log + done + sched + link + relation in one shot
    log                 log CRUD: add / ls / edit / rm — wl log 42 "body" adds (default verb);
                        edit=relog, rm=unlog
    done                mark node DONE + closed_at (multiple ids; --log/--at for one-shot log+done)
    defer               defer a task to a future point (LATER + scheduled_date; fuzzy times
                        supported)
    start               clock-in to start timing (batch ids; --at to backfill past time)
    stop                clock-out to stop timing + compute elapsed (multiple ids; --at to backfill
                        past end)
    spent               record a past time spent (build a clock interval from a duration, good for
                        retrospective entries)
    active              tasks running right now (open clock) + today's elapsed + latest log
    wait                mark WAIT (blocked on others / external input); auto-closes the clock;
                        multiple ids
    reopen              undo DONE/CANCELED/WAIT/LATER back to TODO + clear closed_at (multiple ids)
    cancel              mark CANCELED + closed_at (drop / no-longer-doing; parallel to done);
                        --log/--at supported
    link                link CRUD: add / ls / rm — wl link 42 doc adds (default verb), wl unlink =
                        rm
    unlink              remove one vault-doc link from a node (= wl link rm)
    relation            task↔task relations: block / split / related, +
                        ready/deps/unclaimed/claim/unclaim
    set                 set a value on a node — key-routed shortcut: a prop (= wl prop set) or
                        goal/summary (= wl goal set)
    prop                prop (UDA) CRUD: set / ls / rm (set has the top-level shortcut wl set; rm =
                        wl unset)
    agent               bind the current AI agent session to a task: wl agent <id> (set) / wl agent
                        (show) / wl agent ls / wl agent rm
    unset               remove a value from a node — key-routed: a prop (= wl prop rm) or
                        goal/summary (= wl goal rm)
    clock               clock-interval CRUD: ls / edit / rm (create with start / stop / spent)
    tag                 tag CRUD: add / ls / rm — wl tag 42 +work -planned adds/removes (default
                        verb add)
    show                full detail + timeline for a node (accepts multiple ids)
    node                node primitive CRUD: add / ls / show / edit / rm / reparent (add/ls/show
                        also have top-level shortcuts)
    ls                  list nodes (default limit 20; see shell ls -t / -S / -r-style dimensions)
    tree                tree view of nodes (default: timeline up to today + areas one level, ~30
                        rows)
    focus               focus on a node: upstream path + self + downstream subtree
    ancestors           upstream path: ancestor chain from root to the node
    descendants         downstream subtree: all descendants of a node
    agenda              cross-time-range scheduling overview: everything scheduled in [start, end]
    projects            list active projects + subtask counts + recent activity
    changes             per-project changes in a time window (added / done / log counts)
    summary             time-window aggregate: done/doing/added counts + grouped by project or day
    day                 full view of a day (default today): bucket -> project/plan -> task -> log
    goal                goal CRUD: read/write a node's goal — what you aim to deliver (history-
                        preserving)
    recap               read/write a day's end-of-day summary — what actually happened (history-
                        preserving)
    tick                quick check-in: add a log to each node today (batch habit check-in)
    unlog               delete a log entry: #L<id> exact / --node delete latest that day (undo tick)
    relog               rewrite a log: new body / new time / editor
    retag               change one log's tag (goal / summary / custom; note clears to a plain
                        note)
    metric              structured datapoints (check-in / number / measurement): add/ls/edit/rm
    checkin             interactive check-in of today's habits (default multi-select arrows / space
                        / Enter)
    sched               sched CRUD: add / ls / rm — wl sched 42 2026-06-15 schedules (default verb
                        add); drives wl day 'planned'
    dateinfo            date metadata (holiday/vacation/working-day swap; shown in wl day header)
    date                date-metadata CRUD: set / ls / rm / import (polymorphic shortcut: wl
                        dateinfo)
    alias               manage command aliases: add / ls / rm (e.g. wl alias add w "day -t work" →
                        wl w)
    import              bulk load from JSON ({add:[...],update:[...]}; main AI integration path)
    apply               apply wl-diff lightweight bulk changes (+add/~update/-delete/ anchor; same
                        format as wl output)
    find                full-text search nodes (title/body/log/tag/prop/link, any match)
    reindex             build/update the semantic search index (incremental by default)
    query               semantic search: nearest nodes by meaning (vs find's keyword match)
    logs                list log entries (default last 7 days; preset today/yesterday/week/recent)
    types               list the type./date. classification props in use + counts (raw, grouped by
                        key)
    tags                list every tag in use + a count of nodes carrying it
    props               list every prop key in use + a count (namespaces like github./linear.
                        group)
    metrics             list every metric tag in use + a count of datapoints
    themes              list all color themes (one-line preview per theme)
    help                info-style topic browser: wl help lists topics, wl help <topic> reads one
    print-completion    dump shell completion script (argparse -> fish/bash/zsh; init-load model)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --version             show program's version number and exit
  --db PATH             override the DB path for this invocation (handy for testing / multiple
                        worklogs); takes precedence over $WORKLOG_DB and the XDG default
  --color {auto,always,never}
                        color switch (default auto: enabled on TTY + rich; also reads
                        $WORKLOG_COLOR/$NO_COLOR)
  --theme {auto,dark,light,mono}
                        color theme (default auto: probe terminal bg, pick dark/light; reads
                        $WORKLOG_THEME; see wl themes)
  --width {full,help,N}
                        output width: full (fill terminal, default) / help (cap to the --help width,
                        100) / N columns; also reads $WORKLOG_WIDTH
  --title {wrap,clip}   long node title: wrap (multi-line, hang-indented under the title; default) /
                        clip (one line, truncate with …); also reads $WORKLOG_TITLE
  -q, --brief           brief output: skip log body/timeline/detail in every command, token-saving
                        for AI
  --no-brief            never brief: opt back out of the auto -q that agent sessions get on
                        day/ls/projects/active/summary
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb — wl -o json ls /
                        wl ls -o toon. See: wl help output
  --log-format {oneline,full}
                        log body render style (default oneline = truncate to terminal width with …;
                        full = expand; applies across wl day/tree/logs/show)
  --show-canceled       show CANCELED nodes (hidden by default; --all also includes them)

Concepts (the data model):
  node     everything is one node in a single tree; its type is task · project · area (PARA, below)
           · habit (recurring) · meetlog (meeting note) · day/week/month/… (time)
  log      a timestamped progress entry on a node (each append is kept = history)
  tag      labels on a node; work / personal drive the wl day buckets
  prop     a static key=value attribute (owner, linear-id, …) — single value, overwritten
  goal     a node's goal / summary — history-preserving reserved-tag logs (wl goal)
  metric   a structured datapoint (a number or a check-in) attached to a log
  link     a pointer to an Obsidian vault doc
  sched    schedules a node to a day → it shows up "planned" in wl day
  clock    a time interval (wl start/stop/spent); wl day / active total it
  status   a node's state, shown as a marker: [ ] todo · [/] doing · [x] done · [>] later/deferred ·
           [?] wait (blocked) · [-] canceled
  priority [#A] = P0 (highest) · [#B] = P1 · [#C] = P2 — shown by the id; sorts lists by default

Commands by purpose (run wl <command> -h for options + examples):
  track work    add · log · done · defer · cancel · reopen · wait · tick
  time          start · stop · spent · active · clock
  see it        day · tree · ls · show · logs · find · projects · agenda · summary · changes · focus
  organize      tag · link · sched · set · prop · meta · node · relog · unlog
  plan/reflect  goal · recap · checkin · metric · dateinfo
  bulk & setup  import · apply · init · config · alias · themes · print-completion

Good to know:
  • Organize PARA-style: areas (ongoing responsibilities, no end) ▸ projects (outcomes with
    a finish line) ▸ tasks — set the role with --para area/project (a bare task needs none) and
    nest with --parent <id>.
  • Ids: a node is 42 or #42 (most write-commands take several at once); a log is #L42 and a
    metric is #M7 (as shown by wl show / wl logs) — use those forms with relog/unlog/metric.
  • Dates accept today / yesterday / tomorrow / YYYY-MM-DD, signed deltas +1 / -2d / +3w / -1y
    (number + d/w/m/y, default days), and fuzzy next-week / 2026-Q3 (defer/sched).
  • A task you wl sched to a day shows up "planned" in wl day; logging auto-moves TODO → DOING.
  • Tab-completion: wl print-completion fish|bash|zsh (the command prints setup instructions).
  • Shortcuts: wl add = wl node add , wl set = prop/meta by key; make your own with
    wl alias add w "day -t work" .
  • -q brief output · --db PATH use a different worklog file.
  • Deeper docs: wl help is an info-style topic browser — wl help para (organizing),
    wl help planning (goals/summaries), wl help status, wl help <command>, …

add:
usage: wl add [-h] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [-q] [--no-brief] [--para {area,project,task}]
              [-p {A,B,C}] [-t TAG] [--proj PROJ] [--prop K=V|K] [--parent PARENT] [--status STATUS]
              [--scheduled SCHEDULED] [--sched SCHED] [--deadline DEADLINE] [--body BODY]
              [--log LOG] [--done] [--at AT] [--link LINK] [--relation '<type> <id>…']
              [--metric 'tag [value] [unit]']
              title

Create a new node (task/project/area/meetlog/habit/day/...). Compound flags support add + log + done
+ sched + link + relation in one step, replacing several separate commands. Canonical form:
wl node add (this is the shortcut; see wl node -h ).

positional arguments:
  title                 the node's title, e.g. "ship the Q3 report" (quote if it has spaces)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb. See: wl help
                        output
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)
  --para {area,project,task}
                        responsibility-line role — writes type.para (the same flag as `wl ls
                        --para`). A bare add (no --para) is a loose task with no role; for a time
                        node / soft type / custom type use --prop (e.g. --prop type.date=day, --prop
                        type.habit).
  -p {A,B,C}, --priority {A,B,C}
                        priority: A = P0 (highest) / B = P1 / C = P2
  -t TAG, --tag TAG     comma-separated tags, e.g. -t work or -t work,urgent (work/personal drive
                        bucketing)
  --proj PROJ           project name (stored as a prop)
  --prop K=V|K          set a prop at creation (repeatable), e.g. --prop type.meetlog=dating; bare K
                        (no =) sets an existence prop
  --parent PARENT       parent node id (nest under a project/area), e.g. --parent 103
  --status STATUS       initial status (default TODO); rarely needed at creation
  --scheduled SCHEDULED
                        (rough hint, writes node.scheduled_date) scheduled time: YYYY-MM-DD / YYYY-
                        MM / YYYY-Www / YYYY-Qn / YYYY / someday / tomorrow / next-week / next-month
                        / next-quarter
  --sched SCHED         (precise, writes the sched table = visible as planned in wl day for that
                        date) date: YYYY-MM-DD / today / yesterday / tomorrow / a signed delta +1 /
                        -2d / +3w / -1y
  --deadline DEADLINE   deadline date YYYY-MM-DD
  --body BODY           optional body text
  --log LOG, -m LOG     insert a log entry right after creation (result / output / numbers)
  --done                mark DONE + write closed_at immediately after creation (retrospective task
                        in one shot)
  --at AT               timestamp for --log + (if --done) closed_at (HH:MM / YYYY-MM-DD
                        [HH:MM[:SS]])
  --link LINK           also attach a vault doc (no .md suffix, same semantics as wl link)
  --relation '<type> <id>…'
                        relate the new node to existing one(s), single-write (repeatable); type =
                        block / split / related: --relation 'block 42' / --relation 'split 42' /
                        --relation 'related 42 43'
  --metric 'tag [value] [unit]'
                        attach a structured datapoint (repeatable); reuses the --log carrier or
                        makes one: --metric 'glucose 5.4 mmol/L' / --metric checkin

Common examples:
  wl add "ship the Q3 report"                          # simplest — a task
  wl add "review the PR" -p B -t work --sched today    # priority, tag, plan for today
  wl add "Website revamp" --para project -p A -t work  # a project (→ e.g. #42); --para = the
                                                       type.para role
  wl add "draft the homepage copy" --parent 42         # nest a task under it
  wl add "epic: revamp billing" --relation 'split 42'  # this new node splits out existing #42
  wl add "fixed the login bug" -p B --log "root cause: …" --done --at 14:30   # create + log + close
  wl add "[meetlog] 09:30 tech sync" --prop type.meetlog --parent <day_id>    # a meeting note

agent:
usage: wl agent [-h] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [-q] [--no-brief] {set,ls,gaps,rm,context} ...

Bind the current AI agent session to a node so the agent knows which task it's on and the status
line / hook context can surface it. Stored as an agent_session.<agent> prop on the node (agent =
claude / cursor / codex / …, from $WL_AGENT or --agent, default claude) — no new table.
wl agent <id> is the set shortcut (default verb).

positional arguments:
  {set,ls,gaps,rm,context}
    set                 bind current session to <id>
    ls                  list session→task bindings, most-recently-active first
    gaps                the reverse view: important work (a P0, or a target of today's goal) with NO
                        session bound
    rm                  unbind the current session
    context             machine line <id>\t<title> of the current session's binding (for hooks;
                        empty if unbound)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb. See: wl help
                        output
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)

Common examples:
  wl agent 42             # bind this session to task #42 (default verb: set) — records history
  wl agent 42 --no-record # bind without leaving a history mark (pointer only)
  wl agent 42 --agent codex   # record a non-default runtime (else $WL_AGENT, else claude)
  wl agent                # show what this session is bound to
  wl agent ls             # list all session→task bindings
  wl agent rm             # unbind this session

Two stores, two jobs:
  * the agent_session.<agent> prop is the LIVE pointer — one session → one node, it MOVES on
    rebind, so it always names the node a session is currently on;
  * a HISTORY trail (one log carrying TWO metrics — agent_session = the full session id, and
    agent = the runtime name) stays on the node forever. wl agent <id> writes it BY DEFAULT
    (so auto-binds capture lineage with no flag to remember); --no-record skips it. Recover it
    with wl metric ls <id> --tag agent_session --all (or read wl show <id>'s timeline).

Only the bind event is recorded — later logs don't each carry the session, so it costs one row
per binding, not per write; rebinding the same pair doesn't duplicate it.

Session id: $WL_SESSION_ID, else the runtime's own env var ($CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID /
$CURSOR_CONVERSATION_ID). Runtime name: --agent, else $WL_AGENT, else auto-detected
(e.g. Cursor sets $CURSOR_AGENT=1), else claude.

More: wl help agent.
alias:
usage: wl alias [-h] [-q] [--no-brief] {add,ls,rm} ...

Manage command aliases stored in ~/.config/worklog/aliases.ini. An alias maps a short name to a wl
command, optionally WITH arguments — wl alias add w "day -t work" makes wl w == wl day -t work
(extra args you type are appended); wl alias add d day makes wl d == wl day . Aliases are wired in
at startup, so a change takes effect on the NEXT wl invocation.

positional arguments:
  {add,ls,rm}
    add        add/update an alias (name → command [+ args])
    ls         list configured aliases
    rm         remove an alias

options:
  -h, --help   show this help message and exit
  -q, --brief  brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief   never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand too)

  wl alias add d day            # wl d == wl day (next run)
  wl alias add w "day -t work"  # wl w == wl day -t work (quote a target with args)
  wl alias add p "day -t personal"
  wl alias ls                   # list configured aliases
  wl alias rm d                 # remove an alias

The target's first word must be a real wl command; an alias can't shadow an existing command.
Args you type after the alias are appended (wl w 2026-06-08 → wl day -t work 2026-06-08).

More: wl help alias

usage: wl cancel [-h] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [-q] [--no-brief] [--log LOG] [--at AT]
                 ids [ids ...]

mark CANCELED + closed_at (drop / no-longer-doing; parallel to done); --log/--at supported

positional arguments:
  ids                   node id(s)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb. See: wl help
                        output
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)
  --log LOG, -m LOG     add a log explaining why you're canceling
  --at AT               use this timestamp for closed_at + log

Common examples:
  wl cancel 42                        # drop it
  wl cancel 42 -m "deprioritized"     # close + log reason in one step
  wl cancel 42 --at 2026-05-30 16:00  # closed_at + log use past timestamp

Log-entry CRUD on a node (progress / event stream) — the metric-style entity group.
wl log <id> "body" is the add shortcut (the default verb; auto-progresses TODO->DOING unless
--keep-status). wl relog = log edit , wl unlog = log rm . The full filterable stream view is wl logs
.

positional arguments:
  {add,ls,show,edit,rm}
    add                 add a log entry (= the default wl log 42 "body")
    ls                  list a node's logs (full view: wl logs --id <id>)
    show                show one log entry's full (untruncated) content by log id (#L282)
    edit                rewrite a log's body / time (= wl relog)
    rm                  delete a log entry (= wl unlog)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)

Common examples:
  wl log 42 "result: PR#13 merged"               # progress now (add, the default verb)
  wl log 42 "..." --date yesterday --time 14:30  # backfill a precise timestamp
  wl log ls 42                                   # this node's logs (= wl logs --id 42)
  wl log edit #L282 "fixed"                      # rewrite (= wl relog); wl log rm = wl unlog

More: wl help log (vs wl tick habit check-in / wl logs filterable stream).

                        quick preset: today/yesterday (= --date short form) / week (since Monday) /

  --until UNTIL         YYYY-MM-DD (end)
  --week WEEK           YYYY-Www (ISO week, overrides since/until)
  --month MONTH         YYYY-MM (overrides since/until)
  --quarter QUARTER     YYYY-Qn (overrides since/until)
  --year YEAR           YYYY (overrides since/until)

                        --para`). For non-PARA classifications filter the prop directly: --prop
                        type.meetlog / --prop type.habit / --prop type.date=day
  --status STATUS       filter by status, comma = any-of (TODO/DOING/DONE/WAIT/LATER/CANCELED)
  -p PRIORITY, --priority PRIORITY
                        filter by priority, comma = any-of (A/B/C or P0/P1/P2)
  --prop K=V|K|GROUP.   filter by prop: K=V (exact; matches a member of a comma-joined value) / K
                        (key exists) / GROUP. or GROUP.* (namespace prefix). Repeat for AND, e.g.
                        --prop github.repo=xyb/worklog --prop linear.id
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb. See: wl help
                        output

  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand

  --days DAYS           default window in days when no since/date (default: 7)
  --group {none,day}    day = group by date -> bucket -> task -> log (indented)

  wl logs --id 42 --tail 5            # last 5 logs for one task
  wl logs --since 2026-05-01          # a time window (--since/--until/--week/--month)
  wl logs --by-task --tail 3          # aggregate by task, last 3 per task
  wl logs --group day --by project    # group by day -> project -> task

metric:
usage: wl metric [-h] [-q] [--no-brief] {add,ls,edit,rm} ...

CRUD for metrics — structured datapoints that hang off a log (node → log → metric). A metric has a
tag (what it is: glucose / pullups / checkin …), an optional numeric or text value + unit, a note,
and a timestamp.

positional arguments:
  {add,ls,edit,rm}
    add             add a datapoint to a node
    ls              list metrics: a node's (default this week), OR omit the node to find a tag
                    across ALL nodes
    edit            edit a metric's fields
    rm              delete one or more metrics

options:
  -h, --help        show this help message and exit
  -q, --brief       brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief        never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand too)

Common examples:
  wl metric add 42 glucose 5.4 --unit mmol/L     # a numeric datapoint on node #42
  wl metric add 42 pullups 8 --unit reps         # reps
  wl metric add 42 checkin                        # a pure marker (stored as value 1)
  wl metric add 42 weight 70 --at yesterday       # backfill a timestamp
  wl metric add 42 glucose 6.1 --on-log #L99      # attach to an existing log instead of a new
                                                  carrier
  wl metric ls 42                                 # list node #42's metrics
  wl metric ls 42 --tag glucose --since 2026-06-01
  wl metric edit #M7 --value 5.6 --note "post-meal"
  wl metric rm #M7 #M8                            # delete one or more

A metric must hang off a log; without --on-log a (possibly empty-body) carrier log is created.

migrate:
usage: wl migrate [-h] [-q] [--no-brief]

apply pending SQL migrations from migrations/NNNN_*.sql (auto-run on every command; this is the
explicit form)

options:
  -h, --help   show this help message and exit
  -q, --brief  brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief   never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand too)

The DB version is tracked via PRAGMA user_version. Every migration in
migrations/ is named NNNN_*.sql (numeric prefix sorts the apply order);
files with number > current PRAGMA user_version run in order, each in its
own transaction, then user_version is bumped.

Migrations are auto-applied by ensure_db() on every command, so you
rarely need to invoke this explicitly. Use it to see what's pending or
to retry after a failed migration.

Before applying to an existing DB, the runner snapshots it to a same-dir
<db>.pre-v<N>.bak (N = the version before migrating), so a bad migration
is recoverable. A fresh init (no data yet) is not backed up.

More: wl help migrate
node:
usage: wl node [-h] [-q] [--no-brief] {add,ls,show,edit,rm,reparent} ...

Node CRUD primitives — the metric-style entity group. wl add / wl ls / wl show are the
high-frequency shortcuts onto the same handlers; node edit / node rm / node reparent are the
field-edit / soft-delete / move primitives.

positional arguments:
  {add,ls,show,edit,rm,reparent}
    add                 create a node (= wl add)
    ls                  list nodes (= wl ls)
    show                show a node + timeline (= wl show)
    edit                edit a node's own fields (title/priority/--para
                        role/body/scheduled/deadline)
    rm                  soft-delete node(s) + their spoke rows (reversible tombstone)
    reparent            move a node under a new parent (changes the real parent_id, not a prop)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)

Shortcuts: add → wl add, ls → wl ls, show → wl show (same handlers); edit / rm /
reparent have no top-level shortcut — call them under node.

Common examples:
  wl node edit 42 --title "new" -p A  # edit own fields (not status/parent/tags)
  wl node reparent 42 103             # move #42 under #103 ('none' detaches)
  wl node rm 42                       # soft-delete #42 + subtree (reversible)

reindex:
usage: wl reindex [-h] [--endpoint ENDPOINT] [--model MODEL] [--dimensions DIMENSIONS]
                  [--api-key API_KEY] [--query-prompt QUERY_PROMPT] [-q] [--no-brief] [--full]
                  [--auto]

Embed live nodes (title+body+logs+tags) via the configured embedding server and store the vectors in
a sidecar store. Default = incremental: only new/changed nodes are re-embedded and deleted ones are
evicted. On first run (no index yet) it automatically does a full pass. wl query reads what this
builds. Uses LanceDB if the 'semantic' extra is installed, else a slower pure-Python SQLite fallback
(no extra needed).

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --endpoint ENDPOINT   OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings URL (overrides config/env)
  --model MODEL         embedding model name (overrides config/env)
  --dimensions DIMENSIONS
                        truncate embeddings to N dims (if the model supports it)
  --api-key API_KEY     bearer token for the embedding server, if it needs one
  --query-prompt QUERY_PROMPT
                        query template ({query} placeholder; pass '' to disable) — overrides
                        config/env
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)
  --full                force a full rebuild (drop the index and re-embed every node) — use after a
                        model change or to repair a corrupt index
  --auto                single-flight background worker: hold a lock (skip if one's running) and
                        loop incremental passes until the index is clean. Spawned automatically
                        after a write when [index] auto_reindex is on

  wl reindex --full                   # full rebuild — use after a model change
  wl reindex --endpoint http://host:11434/v1/embeddings --model qwen3-embedding

Vector backend: LanceDB (fast, the optional 'semantic' extra) on any Python 3.9–3.14 on Linux
or Apple-Silicon macOS; falls back automatically to a pure-Python SQLite store where no LanceDB
wheel exists (Intel macOS, musl/Alpine, …) — same results, slower at large scale.

relation:
usage: wl relation [-h] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [-q] [--no-brief]
                   {set,ready,deps,unclaimed,claim,unclaim} ...

Record or list relations between tasks — block / split / related — stored as relation.* props
(comma-separated id lists). Distinct from ancestors (the parent/child hierarchy): relations express
derivation / association / dependency across the tree. Adding is SINGLE-WRITE —
wl relation A block B writes only on A — the reverse (=blocked-by / =split-from , or for related a
one-sided edge folded into =backrels ) is derived at read time, never stored, so it can't go stale.
block edges are checked for cycles at write time — a would-be cycle is rejected, not written. set is
the default verb (the legacy CRUD/list form below); ready / deps / unclaimed / claim / unclaim are
the dependency-query and claim subcommands.

positional arguments:
  {set,ready,deps,unclaimed,claim,unclaim}
    set                 add / list / remove a relation (the default verb, reachable bare)
    ready               frontier: <id> + its block-graph downstream tasks now unblocked
    deps                full (cascaded) dependency graph, optionally scoped to <root>
    unclaimed           open tickets with no active claim, optionally scoped to <root>
    claim               exclusively claim a ticket (fails if held by another, still-fresh claim)

usage: wl unset [-h] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [-q] [--no-brief] id key

Remove a value from a node — the delete counterpart of wl set , key-routed the same way: the key
goal or summary clears that reserved-tag log (= wl goal rm ); any other key removes a UDA prop (=
wl prop rm ).

positional arguments:
  id                    node id
  key                   prop key to remove (or goal/summary → clears it)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb. See: wl help
                        output
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)

Common examples:
  wl unset 42 owner                   # remove the 'owner' prop (= wl prop rm)
  wl unset <node_id> goal             # clear the goal log (= wl goal rm)

Key-routed like wl set: goal/summary → that reserved-tag log, any other key → a prop.

wait:
usage: wl wait [-h] [-o {text,json,jsonl,toon}] [-q] [--no-brief] [-n NOTE] ids [ids ...]

mark WAIT (blocked on others / external input); auto-closes the clock; multiple ids

positional arguments:
  ids                   node id(s)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -o {text,json,jsonl,toon}, --output {text,json,jsonl,toon}
                        output format: text (default) / json (machine-readable) / jsonl (a list
                        streams one object per line, for jq -c / streaming) / toon (compact token-
                        efficient format for LLMs); place before or after the verb. See: wl help
                        output
  -q, --brief           brief output (same as the global -q; accepted after the subcommand too)
  --no-brief            never brief (same as the global --no-brief; accepted after the subcommand
                        too)
  -n NOTE, --note NOTE  add a log explaining what you're waiting on

Common examples:
  wl wait 42                            # mark WAIT (suspended)
  wl wait 42 --note "waiting on review" # add a log explaining what we're waiting on
  wl wait 42 43 --note "waiting on approval" # batch

Note: marking WAIT auto-closes any open clock (WAIT = suspended, no longer timing). Use wl reopen to
revert to TODO.

More: wl help wait
